652.title: All is burning, read whole
652.howItsDone: The Adittapariyaya Sutta, the fire sermon, is studied and chanted in many Theravada communities, and its pattern of the six senses is a common frame for meditation on sense experience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ananda corrected, and your line, the whole of it. Did you reach a good friend? Today we go back to a hilltop from year one and read the whole sermon spoken there. Day six hundred fifty-two.

A thousand men sit on a hill near Gaya. Until recently, every one of them tended sacred fires. They kept their hair matted and twisted, and they poured offerings into flames morning and night, under three brothers named Kassapa. Now they've become monks, followers of the Buddha. And the Buddha, standing on Gaya Head, gives them a sermon in the one language they know better than any other. Fire. Year one told the story. Today we read the sermon itself, the way they heard it. Today: all is burning.
screen: `A THOUSAND MEN ON GAYA HEAD.` → `ONCE, KEEPERS OF THE FIRE.` → `A SERMON IN THEIR LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: SN 35.28 opens: all is burning, monks. And what is the all that is burning? Then it walks through the senses, one by one, with a rhythm meant to be heard. The eye is burning. Forms are burning. Eye-consciousness is burning. Eye-contact is burning. And whatever feeling arises from eye-contact, pleasant, painful or neither, that too is burning. Burning with what? With the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, the fire of delusion. Burning with birth, aging and death, with sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief and despair, I say. Then again for the ear and sounds. The nose and smells. The tongue and tastes. The body and touch. The mind and ideas. Six times the same pattern, until the whole world of experience is on fire. Then the turn. Seeing this, the well-taught disciple grows disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with all of it. Being disenchanted, they become dispassionate. Through dispassion, they are freed. And the text ends: while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of those thousand monks were freed from the taints. Notice what makes it work. It isn't a theory of fire. It's an image these men had lived inside for years. They knew how fire feeds on fuel and goes out when the fuel is gone. The Pali word for that going out is nibbana. The sermon has traveled far. Western readers met it in the nineteenth century, and T. S. Eliot named the third section of The Waste Land, in 1922, The Fire Sermon.
screen: `WHAT IS THE ALL THAT IS BURNING?` · `EYE, FORMS, CONTACT, FEELING` · `LUST, HATRED, DELUSION` · `DISENCHANTED, DISPASSIONATE, FREE` · then, large: `ALL IS BURNING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and if you're somewhere you can, read the sermon's pattern aloud, softly, at the pace of the breath. The eye is burning. Forms are burning. The ear is burning. Sounds are burning. The nose, smells. The tongue, tastes. The body, touch. The mind, ideas. Don't hurry it. Let each line land in the sense it names: look, listen, smell, taste, feel, think. Then sit quietly with whatever is left after the words stop. The bell holds the time.
All is burning. The fire sermon of SN 35.28: the six senses, their objects and feelings, burning with lust, hatred and delusion, and the cooling that comes with letting go. Today's word.
Your line: all is burning. Once today, when a sight or a sound sets you alight with wanting or irritation, notice the fire, and let it have a little less fuel. Day six hundred fifty-two.

screen: `DAY 652 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE EYE IS AN OCEAN.`

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, about to teach a thousand men who've spent their lives tending sacred fires. what image do you use?
fork.reveal: he speaks in the language they know best: everything they experience is burning, and freedom is the fire going out.

original.note: Pali aditta: burning, on fire. SN 35.28 is the Adittapariyaya Sutta, the discourse on burning.

trapdoor: what you thought: all is burning is a warning about destruction.
what it means: in SN 35.28, the six senses, their objects and the feelings they bring are burning with lust, hatred and delusion, and letting go cools them.

what a scholar hears: the sermon belongs to the early story of the community at Gaya, told in the Vinaya's Mahavagga; scholars note how it speaks in the ritual language of fire to former fire-worshippers.

653.title: The eye is an ocean
653.hook: the eye is an ocean for a person, its waves are forms (SN 35.228)
653.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics practice restraint of the senses, guarding the eyes and ears in daily life, and many lay meditators practice noting sights and sounds as they arise without being carried off by them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fire sermon, read whole, and your line, all is burning. Did you give a fire less fuel? Today, the same six senses, but the image turns from fire to water. Day six hundred fifty-three.

You open your phone to check the time. Forty minutes later you surface, a little dazed, holding a stranger's vacation photos and a pair of shoes you didn't need in your cart. You didn't decide to go under. A current pulled, then another, and you went with it. People in the Buddha's day didn't have phones, but they knew the feeling. In one short discourse of the Connected Sayings, he takes the word everyone uses for the vast, dangerous sea and moves it somewhere much closer. Today: the eye is an ocean.
screen: `CHECKING THE TIME.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `A CURRENT YOU DIDN'T CHOOSE.`

segments.voice: SN 35.228 begins with a correction. The untaught person says, the ocean, the ocean. But, the Buddha says, that's not the ocean in the training of the noble ones. That's just a great mass of water, a great expanse of water. Then the real ocean. The eye, monks, is the ocean for a person. Its surge is made of forms, the sights that come at it. Whoever withstands that surge of forms is said to have crossed the ocean of the eye, with its waves and whirlpools, its sharks and its demons. And then he goes through the rest. The ear is an ocean, its surge is sounds. The nose, smells. The tongue, tastes. The body, touches. The mind is an ocean, and its surge is ideas, thoughts, mental objects. Each one has the same dangers. A closing verse says that one who has crossed this ocean, so hard to cross, with its sharks, demons and waves, has gone beyond, and stands on dry ground. Look how carefully the dangers are chosen. Waves knock you over: a sudden sight that grabs you. Whirlpools pull you round and round, like the one we met in the Itivuttaka a few weeks back. Sharks and demons bite: some sights and sounds really do hurt. None of it says the senses are bad. You need eyes to cross a street. The teaching is about the surge, the pull of what comes at the senses, and whether you get swept along. Withstanding is the word. Not closing the eyes. Staying afloat with them open.
screen: `THAT'S JUST A GREAT MASS OF WATER` · `THE EYE IS THE OCEAN, FORMS ITS SURGE` · `WAVES, WHIRLPOOLS, SHARKS, DEMONS` · `STAYING AFLOAT, EYES OPEN` · then, large: `THE EYE IS AN OCEAN.`

segments.voice: Choose one sense for this sit: hearing is a good one. Close the eyes, or let them rest low. Let sounds come: traffic, a fridge, a voice, your own breath. Each sound is a wave. Notice the tug that comes with some of them, toward a story, a judgment, a memory. When you feel the tug, don't fight it. Just stay where you are, afloat, and let the wave pass under you. Then the next. The bell holds the time.
The eye is an ocean. In SN 35.228, each sense is an ocean and its objects are the surge, with waves, whirlpools and sharks; whoever withstands it has crossed. Today's word.
screen: `THE EYE IS AN OCEAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the eye is an ocean. The next time you pick up a screen today, feel for the current before it pulls you under, and decide whether to swim. Day six hundred fifty-three.

what it means: in SN 35.228, each sense is an ocean whose surge is its objects; withstanding that surge is crossing.

what a scholar hears: SN 35 is the Salayatana Samyutta, the chapter on the six sense bases; the same four dangers, waves, whirlpools, sharks and demons, guard the pool in Itivuttaka 109, the river warning from a few weeks back.

654.title: Where is the sound?
654.hook: a king takes a lute apart looking for its sound (SN 35.246)
654.howItsDone: In insight meditation, many Buddhists investigate body and mind part by part, much as the king searches the lute, to see that no single part is the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ocean of the senses, and your line, the eye is an ocean. Did you stay afloat? Today a king hears music for the first time and goes looking for it with an axe. Day six hundred fifty-four.

A king or his minister has never heard a lute. One evening the sound drifts into the palace, and he's captivated. What is that sound, he asks, so lovely, so delightful? His servants tell him: it's a lute, your majesty. Go, he says, bring me that sound. They bring him the lute. And he looks at it, a wooden body, some strings, and says, I don't want this. I want the sound. You can probably feel what's coming. The Buddha tells this story near the end of the chapter on the senses. Today: where is the sound?
screen: `A SOUND IN THE PALACE.` → `BRING ME THAT SOUND.` → `I DON'T WANT THE LUTE.`

segments.voice: In SN 35.246, the servants try to explain. This lute, your majesty, is made of many parts. It has a body, a skin, an arm, a frame, strings, a plectrum. And it sounds because a player puts in the right effort. That's how the sound comes. The king isn't satisfied. He takes the lute and splits it into ten pieces. Then a hundred. Then he burns the pieces, and scatters the ashes in a strong wind, or lets the river carry them off. Then he says: a poor thing, this lute, whatever a lute is. People have been badly misled by it. It's a funny scene, and it's meant to be. The king did exactly what a careful investigator does. He took the thing apart, looking for the place where the sound lives. And it wasn't anywhere. Not in the strings, not in the wood, not in the ashes. The sound was real. It came from the parts and the playing together, and it couldn't be found in any one of them. The Buddha then applies it. In the same way, a monk investigates form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, as far as they go. And when he does, whatever thoughts of I, or mine, or I am he used to have, they no longer come. Notice the parallel with Vajira's chariot a week and a half ago. The chariot was a name for parts. Here it's sound, something you can hear but not hold. The self, the sutta suggests, is looked for in the same way, and found in the same way.
screen: `BODY, SKIN, ARM, STRINGS, A PLAYER` · `TEN PIECES, A HUNDRED, THEN ASHES` · `THE SOUND IS IN NO ONE PART` · `I, MINE, I AM: NO LONGER THERE` · then, large: `WHERE IS THE SOUND?`

segments.voice: Sit, and look for yourself, gently, the way the king looked for the sound. Is it in the feet? The hands? The breath? This passing thought? The feeling in the chest right now? Go slowly, one part at a time. Notice that each part is there, and that something is clearly happening, and that you can't find the one place where you live. No need to conclude anything. Just keep looking, with curiosity, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Where is the sound? In SN 35.246, a king takes a lute apart to find its sound and finds it nowhere, and the Buddha applies the search to the self. Today's word.
Your line: where is the sound. When you hear music today, ask the king's question for a moment, and listen to how it comes from many parts at once. Day six hundred fifty-four.

trapdoor: what you thought: where is the sound is a riddle about music.

what a scholar hears: the vina of the Buddha's time was likely an arched harp rather than today's long-necked vina; the lute simile pairs with the chariot of SN 5.10 as early images for things that are real but not found in their parts.

655.title: The Numbered Sayings
655.hook: teachings arranged from ones to elevens
655.howItsDone: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Anguttara Nikaya alongside the other collections, and many teachers draw on its numbered lists for talks to lay communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a king, a lute and an axe, and your line, where is the sound. Did you listen to the parts? Today we step into the last of the four great collections, and it counts. Day six hundred fifty-five.

Three things to pack for a trip. Five steps to a calmer morning. Seven habits. Ten rules. Lists with numbers in the title get read, and there's a reason: a number gives the mind a shelf. You know when you've got them all. You notice when one is missing. Long before anyone wrote anything down, the monks who memorized the Buddha's teaching knew that too. They gathered a whole collection of discourses and sorted them, not by topic or by place, but by how many items each one listed. Today: the Anguttara Nikaya.
screen: `THREE THINGS TO PACK.` → `A NUMBER GIVES THE MIND A SHELF.` → `A COLLECTION SORTED BY COUNT.`

segments.voice: The Anguttara Nikaya is the fourth of the great collections of discourses in the Pali canon, after the Long, the Middle-Length and the Connected. Its name is usually explained as increasing by one factor. It has eleven books. The Book of Ones holds teachings about one thing. The Book of Twos, two things. The Book of Threes, three. And so on, all the way up to the Book of Elevens. There are thousands of discourses, many of them very short, and many repeat a pattern with small changes, which is how memorizers worked. Why arrange it this way? Partly memory: in an oral tradition, a numbered list is a handrail. If you're reciting the five hindrances and only reach four, you know to look again. And partly use: if a monk was asked to teach about, say, three things to watch, he could go straight to the Threes. Here's a real three, from the Book of Threes, paraphrased. There are three marks of what is conditioned, of anything that's put together. Its arising is seen. Its passing away is seen. And while it lasts, its changing is seen. That's the whole discourse. You could say it on one breath. And yet it's enough to look at a cup of tea, a mood, or a friendship. Over the next weeks we'll read some well-known pages of the Anguttara: a mind that shines, a talk to a doubtful village, a gold-washer, a lump of salt. The numbers are just shelves. The teachings are what sits on them.
screen: `THE FOURTH GREAT COLLECTION` · `ELEVEN BOOKS, ONES TO ELEVENS` · `A NUMBERED LIST IS A HANDRAIL` · `ARISING, PASSING, CHANGING` · then, large: `BY NUMBERS.`

segments.voice: Read one three, right here, with the breath. Bring to mind something simple near you, a cup, a plant, the light in the room, or your own breath. First: its arising. Notice that it came to be, at some point, from something. Second: its passing. Notice that it will end, or is ending already. Third: while it lasts, its changing. Watch for that, the small shifts even now. Arising, passing, changing. Let the three rest in the mind as you breathe. The bell holds the time.
Anguttara Nikaya. The Numbered Sayings: the Buddha's discourses sorted into eleven books by how many things each one lists, from ones to elevens. Today's word.
Your line: by numbers. Pick one thing today, a meal, a meeting, a mood, and see its three: arising, passing, and changing while it lasts. Day six hundred fifty-five.

what it means: a collection of discourses sorted into eleven books by how many items each lists, from ones to elevens.

what a scholar hears: anga means a factor or limb and uttara higher, so anguttara is read as increasing by one factor; its counts of discourses vary between traditional and modern tallies because of the many abbreviated repetitions.

656.title: The luminous mind
656.hook: the mind is luminous, stained by passing visitors (AN 1.51)
656.howItsDone: Meditators in many Buddhist traditions practice noticing moods and defilements as passing visitors, and some, especially in Mahayana and Vajrayana schools, are taught to recognize the clear, knowing nature of mind itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Anguttara Nikaya, sorted by numbers. Did you see something arise, change and pass? Today we open the Book of Ones and find two sentences that Buddhists have been discussing ever since. Day six hundred fifty-six.

A window in winter. Frost on the glass, a smear from someone's hand, dust from the street. From inside, the day looks gray and blurred. Then someone wipes it, and the light comes straight through, and you realize the light was there the whole time. It was the glass that changed. The Book of Ones, the shortest discourses in the Numbered Sayings, has a pair of sentences that sound a lot like that window. They're only a few lines long, and they've kept Buddhist thinkers busy for two thousand years. Today: the luminous mind.
screen: `FROST AND DUST ON THE WINDOW.` → `SOMEONE WIPES IT CLEAN.` → `THE LIGHT WAS THERE ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Here is the passage, paraphrased. Luminous, monks, is this mind. And it is stained by defilements that arrive from outside. The untaught person doesn't understand this as it really is, so for them there is no developing of the mind. Then the pair. Luminous, monks, is this mind. And it is freed from defilements that arrive from outside. The well-taught disciple understands this as it really is, so for them there is developing of the mind. The Pali word for luminous is pabhassara: bright, shining, radiant, a word also used for gold and gems. And the word for the stains is agantuka: arriving, visiting, the word for a guest. Greed, anger, confusion: in this passage they're visitors. They come in. They're not the house. That's the hopeful heart of it. If the stains were built into the mind, training couldn't help. Because they arrive, they can leave, and the mind can be developed. The untaught don't see this, the passage says, and so they don't train. Here Buddhist traditions read the passage differently, and it's worth naming who says what. Theravada commentators often explain the luminous mind as the mind in its resting state between active moments, not a hidden perfect self. Many Mahayana teachers connect it with the idea of buddha-nature, the potential for awakening present in all beings. Some modern scholars point out that the Pali text says very little more than these few lines. All agree on the practical part. The stains are guests. Guests can be shown the door.
screen: `LUMINOUS IS THIS MIND` · `STAINED BY VISITORS FROM OUTSIDE` · `GUESTS, NOT THE HOUSE` · `HOW TRADITIONS READ IT` · then, large: `LUMINOUS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and notice the mood you're in right now. Name it plainly: tired, irritated, flat, anxious, cheerful. Then treat it as the passage does, as a guest. It came in at some point today. Notice where it sits in the body. Now, without pushing it out, look past it, the way you'd look through a smeared window at the light behind. What's there underneath? Maybe just awareness, quiet, noticing. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The luminous mind. Pabhassara: in the Book of Ones, the mind is called luminous, stained by defilements that arrive like visitors, and freed when they go. Today's word.
Your line: luminous. When a bad mood shows up today, greet it as a visitor, not the owner of the house, and look for the light behind it. Day six hundred fifty-six.

the passage is in the Book of Ones

fork.reveal: the passage links understanding this to developing the mind: guests can go, so training helps.

trapdoor: what you thought: the luminous mind is a mind that glows in meditation.
what it means: in AN 1.51–52, the mind is luminous and stained by arriving defilements; understanding this makes developing the mind possible.

what a scholar hears: the Theravada commentary links the luminous mind to bhavanga, the resting life-continuum mind, while Mahayana texts connect related ideas to buddha-nature; the Pali passage itself is only a few lines.

657.title: Know for yourselves
657.hook: to the Kalamas: not by tradition, scripture or logic alone; when you know for yourselves (AN 3.65)
657.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own practice, while traditional teachers also stress that the passage includes checking against what the wise praise.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the luminous mind, and your line, luminous. Did a mood turn out to be a visitor? Today, a confused village asks the Buddha whom to trust, and he answers with questions. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

Kesaputta is a small town of the Kalama people, on a road teachers travel. And the teachers keep coming. Each one arrives, explains his own teaching beautifully, and then tears down everyone else's. Then the next one comes and does the same. The Kalamas are worn out. When the Buddha passes through, they put it to him straight: we have doubts, sir. Which of these people is telling the truth? It sounds like a very modern question: with everyone so sure, how do you know? Today: know for yourselves.
screen: `A TOWN ON THE TEACHERS' ROAD.` → `EACH PRAISES HIS OWN.` → `WHICH ONE IS TELLING THE TRUTH?`

segments.voice: The Buddha starts by agreeing with them. It's fitting for you to doubt, Kalamas. You doubt where doubt is fitting. Then the famous list, paraphrased. Don't go by what's been handed down, or by lineage, or by hearsay. Not by a collection of scriptures. Not by logic, not by inference, not by thinking about reasons, not by a view you've grown fond of after pondering it. Not because the speaker seems capable, and not because you think, this monk is our teacher. Ten things, and notice they include his own authority. But the line doesn't stop at don't. It goes on: when you know for yourselves that these things are unwholesome, blameworthy, criticized by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when taken up, then abandon them. And when you know for yourselves the opposite, then take them up. Then he doesn't lecture. He asks. When greed arises in a person, is it for their welfare or their harm? Harm, sir. Someone overcome by greed kills, steals, goes after another's partner, lies, and gets others to do the same. Does that lead to harm? Yes, sir. Then hatred, the same questions. Then delusion. The Kalamas answer every one themselves, from their own lives. That's the method: not trust me, but look. A modern note. A line often posted online, believe nothing, no matter where you read it or who said it, is a loose modern paraphrase, not the text. The real passage is less sweeping and more useful: check what you're told against what actually helps and harms, and against the wise.
screen: `IT IS FITTING FOR YOU TO DOUBT` · `NOT BY TRADITION, SCRIPTURE OR LOGIC ALONE` · `GREED: FOR WELFARE OR FOR HARM?` · `NOT TRUST ME, BUT LOOK` · then, large: `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and choose one belief you hold about how to live. Small is fine: I need to stay busy to be worth something, or a little anger keeps people in line. Now ask it the Buddha's questions. When I act on this, does it lead to welfare, or to harm? For me? For others? Would the wise people I know praise it, or wince? Don't force an answer. Just look honestly at what happens when you act on it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Know for yourselves. To the Kalamas in AN 3.65: not by tradition, scripture or logic alone, but when you know for yourselves what leads to harm and what to welfare. Today's word.
Your line: know for yourselves. Test one thing you've been told today against what actually happens when you live it. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

original.note: Pali Kalama: the clan of Kesaputta, to whom AN 3.65 is spoken, so it is often called the Kalama Sutta.

trapdoor: what you thought: know for yourselves means trust only your own opinion.
what it means: in AN 3.65, don't rely on tradition, scripture, logic or a teacher alone; test teachings against what leads to harm or welfare, and what the wise criticize or praise.

what a scholar hears: the ten grounds include anussava (oral tradition), pitaka-sampada (a collection of texts) and takka (logic); scholars note the sutta is addressed to non-Buddhists deciding between teachers, and its test is ethical, not a general theory of knowledge.

658.title: Four comforts
658.hook: whether or not there is another world, a kind and clean heart is safe (AN 3.65)
658.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice the four immeasurables, kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, radiating them in every direction, a practice the end of the Kalama Sutta describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Kalamas and your line, know for yourselves. Did you test one belief? Today we read the end of the same talk, the part that's often left out, and close the week. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

Picture the Kalamas after the questions. They've agreed that greed, hatred and confusion lead to harm. But there's a question still hanging in the air, the one the traveling teachers argued about most. What happens after death? Is there another world? Do our deeds bear fruit? Every teacher who came through town had a different answer, and the Kalamas couldn't check any of them. The Buddha doesn't settle the argument. Instead, he describes a person who doesn't need it settled to be at peace. Today: four comforts.
screen: `THE QUESTION STILL HANGING.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER DEATH?` → `A PEACE THAT DOESN'T NEED THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: At the end of AN 3.65, the Buddha describes a noble disciple whose heart is free of greed and ill will, unconfused, mindful. Someone who fills the world in every direction with kindness, compassion, gladness for others, and calm. That person, he says, has four comforts here and now. Paraphrased, they go like this. First: if there is another world, and good and bad deeds bear fruit, then after death I'll arise somewhere good. Second: if there is no other world, and deeds bear no fruit, then here, in this very life, I live free of hostility and trouble, at ease. Third: if evil comes to those who do evil, well, I intend evil toward no one. How could suffering touch me, who do no evil? Fourth: if evil doesn't come to those who do evil, then either way I see myself as clean. Notice the shape. Each comfort has an if. The Buddha, speaking to people who don't yet accept his teaching, doesn't ask them to take rebirth or karma on faith. He shows that a kind and clean heart comes out well on every branch. Elsewhere, the Buddha teaches rebirth and karma plainly, and Buddhist traditions hold them as central. Here, he meets the Kalamas where they are. The Kalamas, the sutta says, were delighted, and went for refuge. Look back at this week. The fire sermon, read whole. The eye as an ocean. A king looking for the sound inside a lute. The Numbered Sayings, by numbers. The luminous mind. Know for yourselves. And now four comforts, for anyone, whatever they believe.

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you love, and let a simple wish for their well-being warm the chest. Then widen it: to people in this building, this street, this city, in every direction, the way the sutta pictures kindness filling the world. Don't force the feeling. Just keep widening the circle, gently. Then rest inside it, and notice: right now, with a kind heart, nothing needs settling. The bell holds the time.
Four comforts. In AN 3.65, the one with a kind, clean heart is at ease whether or not there is another world, and whether or not deeds bear fruit. Today's word.
Your line: four comforts. When a big unanswerable question unsettles you today, come back to what you can do right now: one kind act, one clean choice. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

fork.setup: the Kalamas can't check what happens after death. every teacher says something different. what does the Buddha offer them?
options: a proof that there is another world.
four comforts: a kind, clean heart is safe either way.
fork.reveal: he doesn't settle the argument. he shows that the one with a kind heart is at ease on every branch of it.

original.note: Pali assasa: comfort, solace, assurance; the four assasa of AN 3.65.

trapdoor: what you thought: four comforts are four nice feelings.
what it means: in AN 3.65, four assurances for the one with a kind, clean heart: at ease whether or not there is another world, whether or not deeds bear fruit.

what a scholar hears: some modern readers take the four as Buddhist agnosticism, while traditional commentators read them as skillful teaching to newcomers, since rebirth and kamma are affirmed throughout the canon.
